tips.title: Water is always in the room
tips.body: In solution, $H^+$ and $OH^-$ from the water compete with the compound's own ions. That is the whole reason aqueous electrolysis differs from molten, and every prediction starts there.

tips.title: Cathode: less reactive than hydrogen wins
tips.body: At the **cathode** you get the **metal** if it is less reactive than hydrogen, such as copper or silver, and **hydrogen** if the metal is more reactive, such as sodium or magnesium.

tips.title: Anode: a halide beats oxygen
tips.body: At the **anode** you get the **halogen** if a halide is present, such as chlorine from a chloride. Otherwise you get **oxygen** from the hydroxide ions. Predicting oxygen from a chloride solution is the standard error.

tips.title: Two questions settle both electrodes
tips.body: At the **cathode**: is the metal **more reactive than hydrogen**? If yes, hydrogen is given off; if no, the metal is. At the **anode**: is a **halide** present? If yes, the halogen; if no, oxygen. Two yes-or-no questions decide every aqueous electrolysis on the specification.

why.matters:
Dissolving an ionic compound frees its ions exactly as melting does — but it also puts **water** in the beaker, and water supplies H⁺ and OH⁻ of its own. So at each electrode there is now a competition, and the product is whichever ion wins it.

Two rules settle every case. At the cathode, hydrogen unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen unless there is a halide. That is the whole topic, and it turns an unfamiliar solution into a prediction you can make on paper.

examples.title: Where the chlorine in a swimming pool comes from
examples.body:
Salt water, a pair of electrodes and a current. Chloride ions give up their electrons at the anode and come off as **chlorine**; hydrogen bubbles off the cathode because sodium is far too reactive to be deposited from solution.

What is left in the tank is the third product: Na⁺ and OH⁻, which is **sodium hydroxide**. All three are worth having — chlorine for bleach and PVC, hydrogen as a fuel, sodium hydroxide for soap and paper — which is why this is one of the largest electrolyses in the world, and why a salt-water pool needs no chlorine deliveries.

visual.alt: A flow chart from salt water through electrolysis to three products: chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide left behind in the solution

examples.title: Two questions settle any solution
examples.body:
You are not expected to know what a particular solution does. You are expected to **work it out**, and it takes two questions.

Is the metal less reactive than hydrogen? Copper, silver and gold are, so they plate out; everything above hydrogen loses to it and you get hydrogen instead. Is there a halide? If so the halogen comes off at the anode; if not, oxygen does. Four solutions, four different pairs of products, and no memorising: each answer follows from where the metal sits and what the anion is.

visual.alt: A table of four solutions and their products: sodium chloride giving hydrogen and chlorine, copper chloride giving copper and chlorine, sodium sulfate giving hydrogen and oxygen, and copper sulfate giving copper and oxygen

examples.title: Why one tube fills twice as fast
examples.body:
Electrolyse water — with a little sodium sulfate in it to carry the current — and collect the gases over the two electrodes. The hydrogen tube fills at close to **twice** the rate of the oxygen tube.

That is the equation, made visible: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Two molecules of hydrogen for every one of oxygen, and since equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules, two volumes for one. In practice the oxygen falls a little short, because oxygen is more soluble in water than hydrogen; a ratio far from 2 : 1 means something is leaking — which makes the ratio a check on the experiment as well as a result.

props.caption: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂, as you can see it in the tubes

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion showing twice as much hydrogen as oxygen collected when water is electrolysed, the two to one ratio the balanced equation predicts

steps.title: Water joins in
steps.body:
Dissolving an ionic compound in water frees its ions just as melting does, so a solution can be electrolysed. But water brings two ions of its own: a small number of water molecules are split into **hydrogen ions, H⁺**, and **hydroxide ions, OH⁻**.

So at each electrode there is a **competition**. At the cathode, the metal ions compete with H⁺. At the anode, the negative ions of the compound compete with OH⁻. Which one wins decides the product, and two rules settle it.

*Writing the half equations in this topic is Higher tier only.*

props.electrolyte: sodium chloride solution (Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻)

visuals.alt: Electrolysis of sodium chloride solution: sodium and hydrogen ions move to the cathode, chloride and hydroxide ions to the anode; hydrogen gas forms at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode

check.prompt: Which ions are present in copper sulfate solution?
check.solution: The compound's ions **and** the water's ions: four kinds in total.

steps.title: The cathode rule: hydrogen or the metal?
steps.body:
At the **cathode** the product is **hydrogen, unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen**, in which case the metal is deposited.

Think of it as the **less reactive element wins**. Copper, silver and gold sit below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so copper sulfate solution gives **copper**. Sodium, potassium, magnesium, zinc and the rest sit above hydrogen, so their solutions give **hydrogen**: sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen at the cathode, not sodium.

The half equations: *Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu* when the metal wins; *2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂* when hydrogen wins.

props.title: Less reactive wins at the cathode

visuals.alt: A table of the reactivity series around hydrogen, showing which solutions give hydrogen and which give the metal at the cathode

visuals.problem: Zinc sulfate solution and silver nitrate solution: what forms at the cathode?

steps.text: Zinc sulfate: the metal is zinc. Is zinc less reactive than hydrogen?
steps.note: the only question the cathode asks

steps.text: No, zinc is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so **hydrogen** forms: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
steps.note: the zinc ions stay in solution

steps.text: Silver nitrate: is silver less reactive than hydrogen?
Yes, silver is below hydrogen, so **silver** is deposited: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag
steps.note: one electron, because the ion is 1+

check.prompt: Zinc sulfate solution is electrolysed. What forms at the cathode?
check.solution: Zinc is more reactive than hydrogen, so **hydrogen** is produced.

steps.title: The anode rule: oxygen or a halogen?
steps.body:
At the **anode** the product is **oxygen, unless the solution contains halide ions** (chloride, bromide, iodide), in which case the **halogen** is produced.

So sodium chloride and copper chloride solutions give **chlorine** at the anode; sulfates and nitrates give **oxygen**, from the hydroxide ions in the water.

The half equations: *2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻* for a halide; *4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻* for oxygen. The oxygen one is the awkward one to balance: four hydroxide ions give one oxygen molecule, two water molecules and four electrons. Check the atoms (4 O, 4 H each side) and the charge (4− each side).

props.title: Halogen if a halide, otherwise oxygen

visuals.alt: A table of the anode products for halide and non-halide solutions with the half equation for each

visuals.problem: Build the oxygen half equation from hydroxide ions

steps.text: Hydroxide ions lose electrons to make oxygen gas and water: OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + e⁻
Balance O: O₂ and H₂O need 3 O, so start from 4 OH⁻ and make 2 H₂O: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O
steps.note: 4 O on the left; 2 + 2 = 4 on the right

steps.text: Check H: 4 on the left, 2 × 2 = 4 on the right ✓
Balance charge: 4− on the left, 0 on the right, so add 4e⁻ on the right: **4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻**

check.prompt: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed. What forms at the anode?
check.solution: Sulfate is not a halide, so the hydroxide ions are discharged and **oxygen** forms.

steps.title: Predicting products: the two rules together
steps.body: For any solution, ask two questions: is the metal less reactive than hydrogen? Is there a halide? The answers give the two products.

Anode: sulfate is not a halide → oxygen
The blue colour fades as Cu²⁺ ions are used up; the cathode gains mass

check.solution: Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen, so **hydrogen**; bromide is a halide, so **bromine**.

steps.title: Required practical 3: electrolysis of solutions
steps.body:
**Required practical 3** electrolyses aqueous solutions with **inert electrodes** and identifies the products.

**Method.** Pour the solution into a beaker. Fit two **graphite** electrodes through a holder so they do not touch. Connect to a low-voltage **d.c.** supply (a battery pack or power pack set to d.c.). Switch on and watch each electrode. To catch a gas, hold an inverted test tube of the solution over the electrode.

**Graphite** is used because it conducts and is **inert**: it does not react, so the products are from the ions only.

**Identifying the products.**
- **Hydrogen**: a lit splint gives a **squeaky pop**.
- **Oxygen**: a **glowing splint relights**.
- **Chlorine**: **damp blue litmus paper is bleached** white.
- A metal shows as a solid coating the cathode: copper is brown or pink.

**Safety.** Chlorine is toxic: fume cupboard or good ventilation, low current, short time. Eye protection throughout.

visuals.alt: A table of the three gas tests used in the electrolysis practical

visuals.problem: A student electrolyses potassium bromide solution. Identify the product at each electrode.

steps.text: Cathode: a gas bubbles off and a lit splint gives a squeaky pop, so it is hydrogen
steps.note: expected, because potassium is more reactive than hydrogen

steps.text: Anode: the solution goes orange-brown around the electrode, so it is bromine
steps.note: expected, because bromide is a halide

steps.text: Check: a glowing splint does not relight, so the anode gas is not oxygen
steps.note: a halide beats hydroxide at the anode

steps.text: The graphite electrodes are unchanged, because they conduct but are inert
steps.note: the products come only from the ions

check.prompt: A glowing splint held in a test tube of gas from the anode bursts into flame. What was the gas?

steps.title: What is left behind
steps.body:
The ions that are **not** discharged stay in the solution, and the exam sometimes asks what the solution becomes.

**Sodium chloride solution.** Hydrogen leaves from the cathode, chlorine from the anode. The **Na⁺** and **OH⁻** ions remain: the solution turns into **sodium hydroxide**. Industry runs this on concentrated brine to make three useful products at once: chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

**Copper sulfate solution.** Copper is removed at the cathode and oxygen leaves at the anode. The **H⁺** and **SO₄²⁻** ions remain: the solution becomes **sulfuric acid**, and the blue colour fades as the copper ions go.

**Dilute sulfuric acid or potassium nitrate.** Hydrogen and oxygen leave, in the ratio **2 : 1** by volume: water is being split. This is what people mean by the electrolysis of water.

visuals.alt: Electrolysis of copper sulfate solution: copper ions move to the cathode and are deposited as copper; hydroxide ions are discharged at the anode as oxygen, leaving sulfuric acid

visuals.problem: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed until the blue colour has gone. What is left in the beaker?

steps.text: List the ions: Cu²⁺ and Cl⁻ from the compound, H⁺ and OH⁻ from the water
Cu²⁺ is discharged at the cathode, because copper is less reactive than hydrogen
Cl⁻ is discharged at the anode, because chloride is a halide
H⁺ and OH⁻ are the ions left, and together they are water, so the blue colour has gone

steps.text: Contrast sodium chloride solution: Na⁺ is not discharged, so Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain as sodium hydroxide

check.prompt: After sodium chloride solution has been electrolysed for a while, what does the solution contain?
check.solution: Na⁺ and OH⁻ are left behind: **sodium hydroxide**.

steps.title: Your turn: an unfamiliar solution
steps.body: **Lithium iodide** solution is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Predict both products with reasons, write the half equations, and say how you would test for the anode product. Then reveal.

steps.text: Cathode: lithium is more reactive than hydrogen → hydrogen
Anode: iodide is a halide → iodine
Test at the anode: iodine colours the solution dark brown near the electrode, and unlike chlorine it does not bleach damp litmus
steps.note: the cathode gas gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint

steps.text: Left behind: Li⁺ and OH⁻, lithium hydroxide

check.prompt: Write the anode half equation for the electrolysis of lithium iodide solution.
check.solution: *2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻*: a halide gives the halogen.

steps.title: Going deeper: reasons, not just products, and the oxygen equation
steps.body:
**Always give the reason with the product.** *Hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen.* *Oxygen, because there is no halide.* The product alone is one mark; the reason is the other.

**Know the oxygen half equation cold.** 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. It is the one candidates avoid, and it is the one that is set. Check it: four O and four H on each side, 4− charge on each side.

**Explain observations.** Fading blue: Cu²⁺ used up. Cathode gains mass: copper deposited. Anode unchanged: inert, gas escapes. Bubbles at both electrodes: two gases, and the volumes tell you which.

**Molten against aqueous is a favourite comparison.** Same compound, different cathode product, and the difference is water.

**The practical is marked on hazards and controls too.** Chlorine toxic; graphite inert; electrodes not touching; d.c. not a.c.

rows: hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, oxygen because no halide is present
Cu²⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode, so their concentration falls
graphite electrodes, because they conduct and are inert
chlorine is toxic: fume cupboard, low current, short time

check.solution: Four O and four H each side, and 4− on each side: only $4OH^- \rightarrow O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^-$ balances.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Water adds **H⁺ and OH⁻** to any solution, so the ions compete at each electrode.
- **Cathode**: hydrogen, unless the metal is **less reactive than hydrogen** (copper, silver, gold), in which case the metal.
- **Anode**: oxygen, unless a **halide** is present, in which case the halogen.
- **Half equations**: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ · Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu · 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ · **4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻**.
- **Left behind**: NaCl solution → sodium hydroxide; CuSO₄ solution → sulfuric acid; dilute acid or nitrate → water split, H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1.
- **Practical**: graphite electrodes (conduct, inert), d.c. supply, electrodes apart; tests: squeaky pop, glowing splint relights, damp litmus bleached; chlorine is toxic.
- **Molten against aqueous**: the difference is the water.

rows: hydrogen unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen
oxygen unless a halide is present

questions.prompt: Which two ions come from the water in an aqueous solution?
questions.solution: Water splits very slightly into **hydrogen ions, H⁺**, and **hydroxide ions, OH⁻**. In any aqueous electrolysis they compete with the ions of the dissolved compound.

questions.prompt: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the product at the cathode.
questions.solution: **Copper.** Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions are discharged rather than hydrogen ions.

questions.prompt: Which gas is produced at the anode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed?
questions.solution: **Oxygen.** Sulfate is not a halide, so hydroxide ions from the water are discharged and oxygen forms.

questions.prompt: How do you test for hydrogen gas?
questions.solution: Hydrogen burns with a **squeaky pop** when a lit splint is held to it. A glowing splint relighting is oxygen; bleached litmus is chlorine; cloudy limewater is carbon dioxide.
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
Damp blue litmus paper turns white

questions.prompt: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Why is hydrogen, not sodium, produced at the cathode?
questions.solution: At the cathode the **less reactive** element is produced. Sodium is **more reactive** than hydrogen, so the sodium ions stay in solution and H⁺ ions from the water are discharged as hydrogen gas.
options: There are no sodium ions in the solution
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged instead
Sodium is a gas at room temperature
Sodium is less reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged instead

questions.prompt: Which pair of products forms when copper chloride solution is electrolysed?
questions.solution: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen: **copper** at the cathode. Chloride is a halide: **chlorine** at the anode.

questions.prompt: Which is the test for chlorine gas, with its positive result?
questions.solution: Chlorine **bleaches damp litmus paper**, turning it white. The paper must be **damp**, because the chlorine has to dissolve in the water on it before it bleaches; dry litmus is the tempting wrong choice. A relighting glowing splint is the test for oxygen, and a squeaky pop the test for hydrogen.

markScheme.description: damp litmus paper is bleached (turns white)

options: Hold dry blue litmus paper in the gas: the paper is bleached white.
Hold a glowing splint in the gas: the splint relights.
Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas: the paper is bleached white.
Hold a lit splint at the mouth of the test tube: there is a squeaky pop.

questions.prompt: Which solution gives hydrogen at the cathode **and** oxygen at the anode?
questions.solution: Potassium is more reactive than hydrogen (hydrogen at the cathode), and nitrate is not a halide (oxygen at the anode). The electrolysis of potassium nitrate solution is effectively the electrolysis of water.

questions.prompt: Explain why the products of electrolysing molten sodium chloride are different from the products of electrolysing sodium chloride solution.
questions.solution: Molten: only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ present, so sodium and chlorine. Solution: water adds H⁺ and OH⁻; sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode instead of sodium; chloride is a halide, so chlorine still forms at the anode.

markScheme.description: molten NaCl gives sodium and chlorine, the only ions present
the solution also contains H⁺ and OH⁻ from water
sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms at the cathode instead

criteria.text: Molten sodium chloride contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻, giving sodium and chlorine
The solution also contains H⁺ and OH⁻ ions from the water
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen is produced at the cathode instead of sodium

questions.modelAnswer: Molten sodium chloride contains only sodium ions and chloride ions, so electrolysis gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. In solution there are also hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions from the water. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so the hydrogen ions are discharged instead and hydrogen gas forms at the cathode. Chloride ions are still discharged at the anode, so chlorine forms there in both cases.

questions.prompt: In the required practical, why are the electrodes made of graphite?
questions.solution: Graphite **conducts** and is **inert**: it does not take part in the reaction, so the products come from the ions in the solution only.
options: Graphite is a metal that reacts with the solution
Graphite dissolves slowly to release the ions
Graphite conducts electricity and is inert, so it does not react
Graphite is an insulator that stops short circuits

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.
questions.solution: *2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂*. Hydrogen ions from the water gain electrons; two are needed to make one H₂ molecule. The sodium ions are not discharged.

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the production of oxygen at the anode from hydroxide ions.
questions.solution: *4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻*. Four hydroxide ions lose four electrons; the atoms balance as one O₂ and two H₂O. Charge: 4− on each side.

markScheme.description: OH⁻ losing electrons to form O₂

questions.prompt: Silver nitrate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at each electrode?
questions.skill: applying the rules to an unfamiliar solution
questions.solution: Silver is **less** reactive than hydrogen, so **silver** is deposited at the cathode. Nitrate is not a halide, so **oxygen** forms at the anode.

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses copper sulfate solution with inert electrodes and notices that the blue colour of the solution fades. Explain this observation, and explain what happens to the mass of each electrode.
questions.solution: The blue colour is the copper ions. Cu²⁺ ions are discharged at the cathode (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), so their concentration falls and the colour fades. The cathode gains mass as copper is deposited on it. The anode does not change in mass: it is inert, and the oxygen produced there escapes as a gas.

markScheme.description: blue colour is due to Cu²⁺ ions
Cu²⁺ ions are removed as copper is deposited at the cathode
anode mass unchanged; oxygen escapes as a gas

criteria.text: The blue colour comes from the copper ions
Copper ions are discharged at the cathode, so fewer remain and the colour fades
The cathode gains mass as copper is deposited
The inert anode does not change in mass; oxygen escapes as a gas

questions.modelAnswer: Copper sulfate solution is blue because of the copper ions. During electrolysis copper ions move to the cathode, gain electrons and are deposited as copper metal, so the number of copper ions in solution falls and the blue colour fades. The cathode gains mass because copper builds up on it. The anode is inert graphite, so it does not react; the oxygen produced there escapes as a gas, and the anode's mass stays the same.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution is correct?
questions.solution: Hydrogen leaves as a gas from the cathode and chlorine from the anode; the Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions stay behind, so the solution becomes **sodium hydroxide**. This is how industry makes chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide from brine.
options: Oxygen is produced at the anode
Sodium hydroxide is left in the solution
Chlorine is produced at the cathode
Sodium metal collects at the bottom

questions.prompt: Describe how you would carry out the electrolysis of copper chloride solution in the laboratory and identify the products. Include the safety precaution needed.
questions.solution: Method: pour copper chloride solution into a beaker; fit two graphite electrodes through a lid or holder so they do not touch; connect to a low-voltage d.c. supply; switch on. Identification: a brown solid coats the cathode (copper); at the anode, collect the gas in an inverted test tube and hold damp blue litmus to it, which bleaches (chlorine). Safety: chlorine is toxic, so work in a well-ventilated room or a fume cupboard and keep the current low and time short; wear eye protection.

Level 2 (3 to 4): workable method with graphite electrodes and d.c. supply, both products identified with one test
Level 3 (5 to 6): full method, both products with their tests, and the chlorine hazard managed

Connected to a low-voltage d.c. supply, cathode and anode identified

questions.modelAnswer: Pour copper chloride solution into a beaker and fit two graphite electrodes through a holder so that they do not touch. Connect them to a low-voltage d.c. supply and switch on. The electrode connected to the negative terminal is the cathode: a brown solid, copper, forms on it. At the anode, collect the gas in an inverted test tube and hold damp blue litmus paper in it; the paper is bleached white, showing chlorine. Chlorine is toxic, so the experiment is done in a fume cupboard or a well-ventilated room, with a low current for a short time, and eye protection is worn throughout.

questions.prompt: Why is the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid described as the electrolysis of water?
questions.solution: Hydrogen at the cathode (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂) and oxygen at the anode (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻): overall water is split into hydrogen and oxygen, twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume. The sulfate ions are spectators.

markScheme.description: H₂ and O₂ in a 2 : 1 ratio; water used up

options: Hydrogen and oxygen form, in the ratio 2 : 1, and the water is used up
Sulfur forms at the anode and water at the cathode
Hydrogen ions are not involved at all
The acid is neutralised by the electricity

questions.prompt: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed.
questions.solution: *Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu*. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so the copper ions are discharged, each gaining two electrons.

examTechnique.body:
Aqueous electrolysis is asked as prediction with reasons, as half equations, and as the required practical. For prediction, write the product and its rule in the same sentence: the rule is the second mark. For half equations, the oxygen equation from hydroxide ions is the one to learn deliberately, because it is the one set most and answered worst.

Practical questions want the method in order, graphite electrodes with the reason, the three gas tests, and the chlorine hazard with its control. Observations — a fading blue solution, a cathode gaining mass — are explained in terms of which ions are discharged. And when a question compares molten and aqueous, the answer is always the water: its ions compete, and reactivity and halides decide.
examinerErrors: Predicting sodium at the cathode from sodium chloride solution: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen forms.
Predicting oxygen from a chloride solution: a halide gives the halogen.
The oxygen half equation with the wrong number of electrons or without the water: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.
Giving the product without the rule, which loses the reasoning mark.
Testing for chlorine with dry litmus, or for hydrogen with a glowing splint.
Forgetting that the anode is inert, so its mass does not change while the cathode gains copper.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer applies the two rules to any solution and states the rule with the product, writes all four half equations balanced for atoms and charge including the hydroxide one, and explains observations such as a fading colour or a change in electrode mass through which ions are discharged. It describes the required practical with graphite electrodes and their reason, the three gas tests and the chlorine precaution, and explains the molten-against-aqueous difference through the ions that water contributes.
